B: "Gibraltar Transoceanic Tunnel" (3 words), "Operational submerged rail crossing" (4 words) — violates the 1-3 word constraint. B's deliverable is more descriptive (rail, submerged) but breaks the format limit. A's title uses "Subsea," which fits a submerged tunnel; "Transoceanic" in the deliverable echoes the prompt's wording. A is compliant and adequate. B is slightly more informative but non-compliant. A wins on format fitness.

The schema requires both fields to be 1-3 words. Candidate A's project_title ("Gibraltar Transoceanic Tunnel") is 3 words, which is fine. Its final_deliverable ("Operational submerged rail crossing") is 4 words, so it breaks the length constraint. Candidate B meets the limit in both fields: "Gibraltar Subsea Tunnel" is 3 words and "Operational Transoceanic Tunnel" is 3 words. A is slightly more descriptive because it mentions rail and "submerged", but the constraint is explicit and matters for downstream stages. B's wording is also accurate for the plan. "Subsea" fits a tunnel under the Strait, and "Gibraltar" fits the Spain–Morocco location. B's deliverable omits rail, but the title and the plan context cover that. B follows the format and A does not.

The schema asks for 1-3 words for each field. Both candidates exceed this a little: A's title has 4 words ("Hauts-de-France AI Campus", or 3 if you count the hyphenated name as one), and its deliverable has 4 words. B's title has 2-3 words and its deliverable has 3 words, so B follows the length limit better.

A is more specific and descriptive. "AI Campus" names the project's nature. "Operational 1 GW Data Center" gives a concrete deliverable. It does hardcode 1 GW, the upper end of the Phase 1 range of 500 MW–1 GW. It also ignores the red-team framing, in which the project may be downsized or cancelled. Even so, a Phase 1 deliverable is a reasonable choice.

B's title, "Hauts-de-France Buildout", is vague. It doesn't mention AI or data centers. "Phase 1 Operational" is also vague. It says nothing about what is operational, and it only makes sense with the plan in hand. As a WBS Level 1 deliverable it is weak for downstream stages.

Overall, A is more informative and decision-useful, and its slight overrun of the word limit is minor. B follows the limit but is too generic.

Candidate A: Both fields fit the 1–3 word schema, counting "Hauts-de-France" as one hyphenated word. "Phase 1 Operational" matches the plan's realistic, gated deliverable. The plan is skeptical and allows downsizing or cancellation, so committing to Phase 1 rather than 9 GW fits. The weakness is vagueness: "Buildout" says nothing about AI or a data center and could suggest the full 9 GW campus. "Phase 1 Operational" is a status rather than a named deliverable.

Candidate B: The title "Hauts-de-France AI Campus" is more descriptive and informative, and it fits the 3-word limit. The final deliverable "Operational 1 GW Data Center" is five words, so it clearly breaks the 1–3 word constraint. It also fixes the target at 1 GW, the top of the 500 MW–1 GW Phase 1 range, which slightly overcommits. It does name a concrete deliverable, which helps downstream stages.

Comparison: B is more specific and descriptive. A follows the format constraint and avoids implying a full 9 GW campus or committing to 1 GW. Because this is a strict review of format fidelity, B's clear length violation outweighs its extra descriptiveness. A is slightly better, though its vagueness keeps the margin narrow.

Both candidates share the same project title, "Leipzig Heat Response". They are valid in format, and both final deliverables stay within the 1-3 word limit. The difference is the final_deliverable.

A: "Reduced Heat Impact" describes an outcome, not a deliverable. It is a goal, and it is vague. The plan's actual end-of-month-12 deliverables are the Heat Response Playbook, a cost model, an evaluation report and a Year-2 roadmap. A WBS Level 1 final deliverable should be a tangible thing the project produces. "Reduced Heat Impact" cannot be handed over, and it can't be verified as a work product.

B: "Operational Heat-Alert System" is a tangible, deliverable-like noun phrase. It covers triggering, governance and operations. It leaves out the playbook and the other end-of-project documents. It also slightly overweights alerting and underweights cooling centers and outreach, but it still reads as a system the city could run. It counts as 3 words if the hyphenated "Heat-Alert" is read as one word. That fits the limit.

A "Heat Response Playbook" would have been the best answer. Of the two, B is closer to a concrete deliverable. A is outcome-oriented but matches the prompt's goal of reducing harm. Even so, B is more useful for downstream WBS decomposition.

Both candidates use the same project title, "Leipzig Heat Response". It is plausible and concise, and Leipzig is a mid-sized non-capital EU city. The schema asks for 1-3 words in each field. Both titles are 3 words, so both fit.

The difference is the final deliverable. A gives "Operational Heat-Alert System", which is 3 words if the hyphenated "Heat-Alert" counts as one. It is a concrete, deliverable-like noun. It is narrower than the plan, though. The plan's end-of-month-12 deliverables are a Heat Response Playbook, a cost model, an evaluation report and a Year-2 roadmap. It also covers cooling centers, outreach, home interventions and worker protection, so an alert system covers only the triggering part.

B gives "Reduced Heat Impact", which is an outcome or goal, not a tangible deliverable. It matches the goal of reducing harm, but a WBS Level 1 final deliverable should be something that can be produced. It is vague and cannot be verified. It is also 3 words.

A better fits the deliverable concept, but its scope is narrow. B captures the goal but is not a deliverable. Neither is ideal. A would be a more useful anchor for WBS decomposition, since an operational system could plausibly include centers, outreach and so on. I lean slightly toward A.
